notes: Original substantial narrative and full practice. Open slots: buono, bicchiere and conjunction o; no audio or contracted prepositions. C includes a self-checked personal preference/reason after the question system is taught.

Ada identifies her old reading group without a new past tense. The photograph is a loose small sheet, not a torn page; the blue book stays with the waiting visitors in the library. Her sealed envelope stays on her damaged chair with her friend in the library.
All utterances are divided into distinct speaker turns with original root IDs preserved. Photo-caption positions are schematic; no unknown name besides printed Marco is revealed.

Delivered photo/age, memory, café/offer, drink/glass/bread and good-taste aids accompany first-use stages, with local question/cause form notes. Diagram speech is illustrative and does not add events. No photographic authenticity is claimed for the fictional schematic portrait.

Review 1104-213537-665 corrections: first perché has an immediate known-language reason example, explicitly a margin illustration rather than another plot event. All embedded questions under sapere removed; uncertainty now uses direct attributed dialogue. Photo/pen handoffs made explicit; a5 respondent remains third-person; later question cues reduced to one initial; competing unused pagina distractor replaced by fiore. No new grammar licence or owner checkpoint.

grammar.title: Grammatica
grammar.rule: Cosa? → un libro. Come? → prima guarda, dopo scrive. Quando? → domani. Perché? → perché non ricorda.

rows: Guardo la foto e leggo i nomi.
Perché Lei guarda ancora la foto, Ada?
Guardo la foto perché non ricordo tutti i nomi.

grammar.note_en:
This chapter adds four useful question words. Cosa asks “what”: Cosa guarda Ada? means “What is Ada looking at?” The answer names an object, la foto. Earlier chi asks “who” and dove asks “where”; compare Chi è Marco? (“Who is Marco?”), Dove è Marco? (“Where is Marco?”), and Cosa scrive Paolo? (“What does Paolo write?”). Keep the question’s information gap clear rather than translating every question with one English-shaped pattern. No new object pronoun is needed in these examples.

Come asks “how”. It can request a description, Come è il caffè? (“What is the coffee like?”), answered with È buono (“It is good”). It can also request a method: Come cerchi il nome? means “How do you look for the name?” Paolo answers with an ordered action, first looking below the photograph and then writing on his sheet. These uses share the question word but request different kinds of answer. Quando asks “when”: Quando partite? means “When are you leaving?”; domani, tomorrow, supplies the time. Quando cerchiamo Marco? asks when the search takes place, without teaching a future-tense paradigm.

Perché has two roles. In a question it means “why”: Perché Ada non parla? asks for a reason. In an answer or statement it means “because”: Guardo la foto perché non ricordo tutti i nomi means “I look at the photograph because I do not remember all the names”. The written accent belongs to perché in both roles. A perché answer gives a reason, whereas a quando answer gives a time. Because it is a reason, the information after perché should explain the action rather than merely repeat it.

The verbs keep the present forms already learned. Ricordo/ricorda mean “I remember / remembers”; the photograph and its names help Ada remember her former reading group. Calling it il mio vecchio gruppo, “my old group”, does not introduce a past-tense verb form. The scene identifies the people in an old photograph and what Ada remembers now; it does not yet narrate their past meetings. The familiar leggono and libri identify what the people do together in the photograph. Tempo here is available time, not weather: abbiamo tempo, “we have time”.

New practical examples are io bevo, tu bevi, Elena beve, voi bevete (“I drink, you drink, Elena drinks, you drink”, plural); io mangio, tu mangi, Paolo mangia, voi mangiate (“I eat, you eat, Paolo eats, you eat”, plural). Bere has an irregular stem here, bev-. Offro un caffè means “I offer a coffee” and, in this social context, “I treat you to a coffee”; Ada offre means “Ada offers/treats”. The chapter does not teach paying vocabulary or a command form. Buono/buona describe something good to taste; o connects alternatives, “or”. Formal Lei continues with third singular: Lei beve and Lei ricorda. The personal final question uses the familiar singular preferisci to address the learner.
